description: Yvy Hendy («tierra encendida» en guaraní) es un equipo de Ciudad del Este especializado en análisis geoespacial y teledetección. Abordamos el desafío de armonización de focos de calor MODIS y VIIRS para construir un calendario interactivo de quemas en Paraguay, que compare la temporada en curso con su comportamiento histórico y apoye la gestión del fuego por bomberos, gobiernos locales e instituciones ambientales. Equipo completo.
summary:
Yvyhendy is a public web platform that turns NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent record of fire activity in Paraguay, from November 2000 to today. MODIS and VIIRS see fire very differently: VIIRS has finer pixels and detects many more hotspots, so simply adding the two makes the count jump every time a new satellite is launched. In Paraguay the raw total rises 274% in 2012, when S-NPP enters, and 71% in 2023, with NOAA-21, without any real increase in burning.
We built a harmonization method that expresses every detection as a MODIS-equivalent count on a 0.1° grid, month by month and day by day, and we validated it against independent burned-area products. After harmonization those artificial jumps fall below 2%. The platform updates itself every four hours with near-real-time data and lets anyone explore the map, compare any period with the 2001–2020 normal, see confirmed fires, download data for GIS, and ask an assistant in plain Spanish or English.
This matters because fire policy, prevention budgets and public debate in Paraguay depend on knowing whether a season is truly worse than usual. A series that changes with the sensor cannot answer that question; a harmonized one can.
details:
What it does

Yvyhendy answers three practical questions for Paraguay: where is it burning now, how does this compare with a normal year, and where should prevention be focused. To do that it combines a harmonized historical record with live detections in one interface:

  • Geospatial explorer: live hotspots from the last days on an interactive map, with density and intensity views, district and department filters, and a detail card for each detection (fire radiative power, satellite, time and confidence).
  • Harmonized history: 313 months of comparable data, with daily, weekly, monthly and yearly calendars that show each period against the 2001–2020 median.
  • Prevention tools: a seven-day statistical outlook of expected hotspots by department, weather layers, protected areas and indigenous territories, and indicative firebreak proposals where recurrent fire meets an area worth protecting.
  • Confirmed fires: a separate layer for field reports with photo, place, date and source. They always enter as "under verification" and are never mixed with satellite detections.
  • Open data: downloads in CSV, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, Shapefile, KML and Excel, ready for QGIS.
  • Hendy, the assistant: answers questions in natural language using live data from NASA FIRMS, the weather forecast and the harmonized series.

How it works

The core of the project is the harmonization pipeline. It runs automatically on GitHub Actions and every result is published with its checksums so it can be reproduced. It follows four steps:

  1. Clean input. We use NASA FIRMS detections from MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21). We keep only points inside Paraguay, drop low-confidence and industrial sources, give priority to the standard science product over near-real-time data, and remove duplicates.
  2. A common VIIRS scale. All VIIRS sensors are brought to the NOAA-20 scale using the months in which they fly together: S-NPP × 0.857 (99 shared months, 90% CI 0.844–0.864) and NOAA-21 × 1.006 (45 shared months).
  3. MODIS equivalent. We tested three converters (a global ratio, a ratio by department and month, and a Poisson gradient-boosting model) and selected the one with the lowest error in leave-one-year-out validation: the global ratio. For 2000–2002, when only Terra was flying, a monthly correction of about × 2.5 is applied.
  4. Fusion and daily detail. MODIS and VIIRS are combined by inverse-variance weighting that carries the uncertainty of each sensor (φ = 0.05). The monthly result is then distributed to individual days: all 313 months have daily detail, and the days add up to 99.96% of the monthly totals.

On top of this record, the web application (Next.js and MapLibre) adds live FIRMS detections every four hours, the Open-Meteo forecast, and protected-area and territory layers queried directly from their official services. An automatic audit compares the harmonized totals with the official FIRMS counts on every update and publishes the result inside the platform.

Benefits

  • Comparable years. Agencies, journalists and researchers can say whether a season is above or below normal without the sensor change distorting the answer.
  • Early action. Live detections, the seven-day outlook and weather layers help prioritize where to look first.
  • Protection of sensitive areas. Firebreak proposals and protected-area layers point to the edges where recurrent fire threatens forests and indigenous lands.
  • Transparency. The method, the validation and the data are open. Every number in the platform says where it comes from, and satellite detections are never presented as confirmed fires.

What we hope to achieve

We want Yvyhendy to become a reference tool for fire management in Paraguay, used by the institutions in charge of prevention, municipalities, firefighters, students and communities. The method is not tied to one country: the same steps can be applied to any region covered by MODIS and VIIRS. Our next goals are to extend the harmonization to the whole of South America and, later, to the global record, and to add historical weather variables to the seven-day outlook.

Challenges we faced

The only real difficulty we faced was not having access to more powerful computing equipment. Harmonizing the series at a global scale means processing more than two decades of detections from five satellites for the whole planet, and that was beyond the hardware available to our team during the hackathon. For that reason we focused on Paraguay, where the harmonized series, the validation and the platform are complete and working. The method and the code are ready to scale as soon as we have adequate computing resources.

Tools and technologies

  • Data processing: Python (pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, PyArrow, scikit-learn), automated with GitHub Actions.
  • Web platform: TypeScript, Next.js and React, MapLibre GL for maps, ECharts for charts; hosted on Vercel.
  • Data storage: Hugging Face Datasets for the processed hotspot archive.
  • GIS: QGIS and GDAL for checking layers and exports.
  • Assistant: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 models through the NVIDIA API, connected to live data tools.
